analysis.headline: Passed the House 357-70 on January 31, 2024, but Senate cloture on the motion to proceed failed 48-44 on August 1, 2024, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have expanded the refundable child tax credit for low- and moderate-income families, sped up tax deductions businesses could take for research costs and equipment purchases, made disaster and East Palestine, Ohio train derailment relief payments tax-free, expanded the low-income housing tax credit, and raised penalties on promoters of questionable COVID-era employee retention credit claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income families with children (through a larger refundable child tax credit of up to $1,800-$2,000 per child for 2023-2025 [S3]); victims of federally declared wildfires and the East Palestine train derailment, whose relief payments would have been excluded from taxable income [S3] [S5]; developers and tenants of new affordable housing through a bigger low-income housing tax credit [S3]; and businesses through immediate expensing of domestic research costs, restored 100% bonus depreciation, and higher Section 179 expensing limits [S3] [S5].

how_it_helps.text: Multiplies the refundable child tax credit by the number of qualifying children and raises the maximum refundable amount to $1,800 (2023), $1,900 (2024), and $2,000 (2025), with inflation indexing — directly increasing cash refunds for working families with low tax bills [S3] [S5].
Lets taxpayers with an income drop elect to use prior-year earned income when calculating the earned income tax credit in 2024 and 2025, protecting families whose wages fell [S3].

Excludes from gross income compensation for losses from federally declared wildfires (payments received after 2019) and from the February 3, 2023 East Palestine, Ohio train derailment, so victims would not owe tax on relief payments [S3] [S5].

Raises the low-income housing tax credit ceiling by 12.5% for 2023-2025 and lowers the bond-financing threshold to 30% for projects financed by bonds issued before 2026, supporting construction of more affordable rental housing [S3] [S5].

Allows businesses to immediately expense domestic research costs incurred 2022-2026, extends 100% bonus depreciation through 2026, and raises Section 179 expensing limits to $1.29 million, which supporters argued would encourage investment and hiring [S3] [S5].

Raises penalties on promoters who aid understatement of tax liability through questionable COVID employee retention credit claims, including a penalty of the greater of $200,000 or 75% of gross income derived from the promotion [S3] [S5].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury bears the cost, since the bill combines tax cuts for families with large business tax breaks (R&D expensing, bonus depreciation, business interest limits) without offsets identified in the CRS summary [S3]. Promoters of COVID employee retention credit claims face sharply higher penalties and a January 31, 2024 cutoff on retroactive claims [S5]. The Taiwan provisions would reduce U.S. withholding tax rates (from 30% to 10% in most cases) on certain Taiwan investors' U.S.-source income [S5].

drawbacks.text: The business provisions are the largest part of the bill: immediate R&D expensing, bonus depreciation, and higher expensing limits primarily reduce taxes for corporations and business owners, not households, and the CRS summary identifies no revenue offsets for the package [S3].
The child tax credit expansion is temporary — the higher refundable amounts run only through 2025, though the $2,000 amount is indexed to inflation afterward [S3] [S5].
Section 602(h) bars any credit or refund of COVID employee retention tax credits after January 31, 2024 unless a claim was filed by that date, cutting off businesses that had not yet filed [S5].

Raising the 1099 information-reporting threshold from $600 to $1,000 reduces third-party reporting that helps the IRS detect unreported income, a trade-off acknowledged by the title's own framing as tax administration relief [S3] [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The family, disaster, and housing provisions deliver tangible benefits to ordinary people — larger refunds for low-income working families and tax-free disaster payments — while the majority of the package's fiscal cost goes to business tax breaks with no identified offsets, making the bill a mixed package rather than a clean pro-family measure. The Temporary business tax cuts also build in pressure for future extensions, which historically add to long-term deficits.

outcome.mechanism: Cloture on the motion to proceed to the measure failed in the Senate 48-44 (60 votes needed) on August 1, 2024, and the bill never received a Senate floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill under suspension of the rules (requiring a two-thirds majority) by 357-70 on January 31, 2024, with 188 Democrats and 169 Republicans voting yes [S7] [S8].
The Ways and Means Committee reported the bill amended by a 40-3 vote on January 19, 2024, just two days after introduction [S7].
The Senate received the bill on February 1, 2024, read it twice, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 349) on March 21, 2024 [S7].

On July 29, 2024, a motion to proceed to consideration was made and a cloture motion was presented; on August 1, 2024, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 48-44, with 43 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 2 Independents voting yes and 41 Republicans, 1 Democrat, and 2 Independents voting no [S7] [S10].
The bill received no further Senate action and died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S7].

key_actors.name: Senate Republicans (41 voting no)
key_actors.what_they_did: Cast 41 of the 44 votes against cloture on the motion to proceed to the bill on August 1, 2024, denying the 60 votes needed to begin consideration [S10].

key_actors.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
key_actors.what_they_did: Brought the motion to proceed and filed cloture on July 29, 2024, and moved to reconsider after the failed cloture vote on August 1, 2024 [S7].

key_actors.name: Rep. Jason Smith
key_actors.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
key_actors.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, moved to suspend the rules and pass it in the House, and guided it through committee markup (reported 40-3) and floor passage 357-70 [S7] [S8].

key_actors.name: House members voting yes (357)
key_actors.what_they_did: Passed the bill 357-70 under suspension of the rules on January 31, 2024 [S8].
